(p-371) Surah "Adh-Dhariyat"

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

﴿By the winds that scatter,﴾ (al-Dhariyat, meaning the winds), because they scatter the dust and other things. Reading the taʾ (ت) as assimilated into the dhal (ذ) is the reading of Hamzah and Abu ʿAmr.

﴿scattering⁠ ⁠﴾ (dharwan) is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the word governing it is the active participle (ism al-fa'il).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 2:

﴿Then those that carry the burden﴾: (al-ḥāmilāt) are the clouds, because they carry the rain.

﴿A heavy load﴾ (wiqran) is the object (maf'ūl) of (al-ḥāmilāt).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 3:

﴿Then those that glide﴾, [i.e., the ships (al-fulk)],

﴿with ease﴾: a gliding that is easy (dhū yusr), i.e., [moving] with facility (dhū suhūla).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 4:**

﴿Then those who distribute by command﴾: the angels, because they distribute affairs, [such as] rain, provisions, and other things. Or they carry out the distribution while commanded to do so. Or they take charge of distributing the affairs of the servants. So Jibril is for harshness, Mika'il is for mercy, the Angel of Death is for seizing souls, and Israfil is for the blowing [of the Trumpet]. It is also permissible that what is meant is the winds alone, because they produce the clouds, carry them, direct them, move through the air with an easy movement, and distribute the rain by turning the clouds. The meaning of the فاء (fa', the particle "then") according to the first view is that He swore by the winds, then by the clouds that they drive, then by the ships that they make run by their blowing, then by the angels who distribute provisions by Allah's permission, [namely] the rain and the commerce of the sea and its benefits. Or, according to the second view, [the meaning is] that they begin to blow, scattering the dust and pebbles, then they carry the clouds, then they move through the air spreading them out, then they distribute the rain.

﴿Indeed, what you are promised﴾ [al-An'am: 134] is the response to the oath (jawab al-qasam). The "ma" is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah), or a verbal particle (masdariyyah). What is promised is the resurrection (al-ba'th).

﴿is surely true﴾: it is a true promise, like "a pleasing life" (ʿīshatun rāḍiyatun), meaning one possessing contentment.

﴿And indeed the Recompense﴾: the requital for deeds,

﴿is surely going to occur﴾: is certainly going to happen.

(p-372) ﴿By the heaven﴾: this is another oath.

﴿Full of paths﴾ (dhāt al-ḥubuk): the fine, well-formed paths (ṭarā'iq ḥasanah), like what appears on water from the blowing of the wind. Likewise, "ḥubuk al-sha'r" (the waves/wrinkles of hair) are the traces of its curling and bending. It is the plural of ḥabīkah, like ṭarīqah and ṭuruq (paths). It is said that the creation of the heaven is also like this. And from al-Ḥasan: "its ḥubuk are its stars," being the plural of ḥibāk.

ـ﴿Indeed, you are in a varying opinion.﴾ That is, their saying about the Messenger: "a sorcerer," "a poet," and "a madman," and about the Qur'an: "sorcery," "poetry," and "legends of the former peoples."

Verse 9: ﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an or to the Messenger, meaning: whoever is turned away from it is turned away with the turning that has no more severe or greater turning than it. Or it means: whoever is turned away from it is one who was turned away in the pre-eternal knowledge of God, i.e., He knew from eternity that he is turned away from the truth, one who does not desist. It is permissible that the pronoun refers to "what you are promised" (ma tu'adun), or to the religion (al-din). He swore by the scatterers (al-Dhariyat) that the occurrence of the matter of the Resurrection is true; then He swore by the sky that they are in a discordant saying regarding its occurrence: some of them are doubtful and some of them are deniers. Then He said: whoever is turned away from acknowledging the matter of the Resurrection is the one who is turned away.

﴿قُتِلَ﴾ (Qutila), meaning "was cursed" (lu'ina). Its origin is a supplication for killing and destruction, and then it came to be used in the same way as "lu'ina" (was cursed).

﴿الخَرّاصُونَ﴾ (al-kharrasun), meaning "the liars" (al-kadhdhabun), those who conjecture what is not sound. They are the people of the divergent speech, and the lam (al-lam, the definite article) is a pointer to them. It is as if it were said: "Cursed are these liars (al-kharrasun)."

Ask: they say, "When is the Day of Judgment?" That is, when is the Day of Recompense? Its implied meaning is: "When is the occurrence of the Day of Judgment?", because times (aḥyān) are only used as adverbial modifiers (ẓurūf) for events (ḥudthān). The word "yawm" (day) in the answer is in the accusative by means of a hidden verb, indicated by the question, meaning: "it occurs."

Note: The verse under discussion is 51:12, "They ask, 'When is the Day of Judgment?'" (﴿يَسْألُونَ أيّانَ يَوْمُ الدِّينِ﴾).

Translation:

"[It will be] on the Day when they will be tormented over the Fire." It is permissible for it (yawm) to be in the fatḥah (fatha) form because it is attached to something indeclinable (mutamakkin, i.e., not fully inflected for case), namely the clause (jumlah). Its position (maḥall) is in the accusative (naṣb) by the hidden verb which is "yaqa'u" (it will occur), or in the nominative (raf') by [an implied sentence meaning] "He is the Day when they will be tormented over the Fire", i.e., they will be burned.

(p-373) ﴿Taste your trial﴾: that is, the keepers of the Fire will say to them, "Taste your punishment and your burning in the Fire."

﴿This﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿that which﴾: that is, this punishment is that which ﴿you used to seek to hasten﴾ in the world, by your saying, "Bring us what you threaten us with." Then he mentioned the state of the believers, saying:

Verily the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs. (That is) to say: the springs, which are the flowing rivers, will be such that they see them and their eyes fall upon them, not that they are within them.

Accepting what their Lord has given them, receptive to all the reward He has bestowed upon them, content with it. "Accepting" (ākhidhīna) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in the adverbial expression (ẓarf), which is the predicate (khabar) of "inna" (indeed).

﴿Indeed they were before that﴾, before entering Paradise in the world (al-dunyā),

﴿doers of good (muḥsinīn)﴾, they had done their deeds well. The explanation of their good-doing is what follows:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 17:

﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾, i.e., they slept. The "mā" is an extra particle (zā'idah) for emphasis (tawkīd). "Yahja'ūn" is the predicate (khabar) of "kānū", and the meaning is: "They used to sleep during a small portion of the night." Or "mā" is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), and the estimate is: "They were little of the night in their sleeping (hujūʿuhum)," so that "hujūʿuhum" is in the nominative because it is a substitute (badal) for the waw in "kānū", not governed by "qalīlan," since it has become described by his saying "of the night." It left the resemblance of a verb, and its governing function is by way of resemblance, meaning: "Their sleeping was little of the night." It is not permissible for "mā" to be a negating particle (nāfiyah), with the meaning that they do not sleep during a small part of the night, and spend all of it in worship, because the negating "mā" does not govern what comes after it over what comes before it. You do not say: "Zaydan mā ḍarabtu" (Zayd, I did not strike).

"And in the hours before dawn they seek forgiveness."

He described them as those who spend the night in worship, rising to pray during it. When they reach the pre-dawn hours (al-asḥār), they turn to seeking forgiveness, as though they had committed sins during their night.

"Al-saḥar" (the pre-dawn period): the last sixth of the night.

And in their wealth there was a right for the beggar (al-sa'il), that is, for the one who asks because of his need,

and the deprived (al-mahrum): that is, the one who presents himself (for help) but does not ask, out of modesty.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 20:

﴿And in the earth are signs﴾, which point to the Maker (al-Sani'), His power, His wisdom, and His governance (tadbir), since it is spread out (madhuwwa) like a carpet for what is above it, and in it are paths and broad roads (fijaj) for those who move about upon it. It is divided (mujazza'a): some of it is plain and some mountainous; it is firm and soft, rugged (ʿadhah) and salty (sabakha). In it are gushing springs, crumbling minerals, and scattered creatures (dawabb munbaththa), differing in forms and shapes, varying in states and actions.

﴿for those who have certainty﴾, for the monotheists who have taken the straight, demonstrative path (al-tariq al-sawiyy al-burhani) that leads to knowledge (ma'rifa). They are contemplators with seeing eyes and penetrating understandings; whenever they see a sign, they know the manner of reflecting upon it, and so their certainty increases upon their certainty.

﴿And in yourselves﴾: in their beginning and their state, and their transition from one condition to another, and in their inner and outer aspects, are wonders of creation and marvels of making, at which minds are bewildered. It is enough for you to consider the hearts and what intellect has been set within them, and the tongues, speech, and the points of articulation of the letters, and what there is in their composition, arrangement and subtleties of clear signs and decisive proofs of the wisdom of their Arranger and Maker. Leave aside the ears, the eyes, the limbs, and all the members, and their fitness for what they were created for, and the joints that were placed in the limbs for bending and flexing; for when any of them becomes stiff, incapacity comes, and when it becomes slack, humiliation settles in. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators. As for what has been said, that the implied sense is "Will you not see in yourselves?", it is weak, because it leads to placing what falls within the scope of the interrogative before the interrogative particle.

﴿Will you not see?﴾: you look with the look of one who takes heed.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 22:

﴿And in the sky is your provision﴾, i.e., the rain, because it is the cause of sustenance (al-aqwat). It is related from al-Hasan that whenever he saw clouds he would say to his companions: "By Allah, in it is your provision, but you are deprived of it because of your sins,"

﴿and what you are promised﴾: Paradise. It lies above the seventh heaven, beneath the Throne. Or he meant: what you are given as provision in this world, and what you are promised in the Hereafter, all of it is decreed and written in the sky.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 23:

﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, it is indeed the truth, just as it is true that you speak.﴾ The pronoun (in innahu, "it") refers either to the provision (al-rizq) or to "what you are promised" (ma tu'adun).

"Mithla ma annakum tantiqun" (just as you speak): with the nominative (bi-l-raf'), it is read by the Kufans other than Hafs as an attribute (sifah) of "al-haqq" (the truth), meaning: "a truth like your speech." The others read it in the accusative (bi-l-nasb), meaning: "indeed it is the truth, like your speaking." It is also permissible that it be read with a fatha (fathan) because it is annexed (idafah) to a non-declinable word (ghayr mutamakkin), and "ma" is superfluous (mazidah).

It is related from al-Asma'i that he said: "I was coming from the mosque of Basra, when a Bedouin appeared on a young camel, and said: 'Who is the man?' I said: 'From the Banu Asma'.' He said: 'Where have you come from?' I said: 'From a place where the speech of Allah is recited.' He said: 'Recite to me.' So I recited: ﴿Wa-l-dhariyat﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 1]. When I reached His saying: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 22], he said: 'That is enough for you.' He got up to his she-camel, slaughtered her, and distributed her among those who came and went, and he went to his sword and his bow, broke them both, and departed. When I performed the pilgrimage with al-Rashid, I began to circumambulate, when suddenly someone called out to me in a gentle voice. I turned, and behold, it was the Bedouin, emaciated and yellowed. He greeted me and asked me to recite the surah. When I reached the verse, he cried out and said: 'We have found what our Lord promised us to be true.' Then he said: 'Is there anything other than this?' So I recited: ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, it is indeed the truth﴾. He cried out and said: 'Glory be to Allah! Who is it that angered the Majestic until He swore? They did not believe Him with His word until He swore.' He said it three times, and his soul departed with it."

﴿Has the story come to you?﴾ This is an expression of magnification of the account, and an alert that it is not from the knowledge of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Rather, he knew it through revelation (wahy, divine inspiration). Its connection with what precedes it lies in His saying, "And on the earth are signs," and His saying at the end of this story, "And We left in it a sign."

﴿The story of Abraham's guests﴾. "Al-ḍayf" (الضَّيْفُ, "the guest") is used for both the singular and the plural, like "al-ṣawm" (الصَّوْمُ, "the fast") and "al-zawr" (الزُّورُ, "the falsehood"), because in origin it is a verbal noun (maṣdar, the noun of action) of "ḍāfahu" (ضافَهُ, "he hosted him"). They were twelve angels. It is also said they were nine, the tenth being Gabriel. He called them "guests" because they appeared in the form of guests, since Abraham hosted them, or because they were regarded by him as guests.

﴿The honored ones﴾, with God, based on His saying, "Rather, they are honored servants" [al-Anbiya: 26]. It is also said that it is because he served them himself, had his wife serve them, and hastened to provide them with hospitality.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 25:

﴿When they entered upon him﴾: it is governed by "al-mukramin" (the honored guests), if it is interpreted as Ibrahim's honoring of them; otherwise it is governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember).

﴿Then they said, "Peace"﴾: "salaman" is a verbal noun (masdar) that stands in place of the verb, being used instead of it, and its original form is "nusallimu 'alaykum salaman" (we greet you with peace).

﴿He said, "Peace"﴾, meaning: "'Alaykum salam" (peace be upon you). It is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted. (p-376) The shift to the nominative serves to indicate the establishment of peace, as if he intended to greet them with something better than what they had greeted him with, following the courtesy of Allah. This too is part of his honoring of them. Hamza and 'Ali (read): "silm" (with a kasra), and "al-silm" means "al-salam" (peace).

﴿"A people unknown"﴾, meaning: you are a people unknown to me, so inform me who you are.

Translation:

﴿So he turned quietly to his family⟩, and went to them secretly from his guests. It is part of the courtesy of the host that he conceal his intention and hasten to the hospitality without the guest perceiving it, lest the guest should refuse it. The bulk of Ibrahim's (peace be upon him) property was cattle,

﴿Then he brought a fatted calf﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 27:

﴿So he brought it near to them﴾, that they might eat from it, but they did not eat.

﴿He said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ He rebuked them for leaving the food uneaten, or urged them to eat it.

﴿So he conceived fear﴾ (fa-awjasa): he concealed it, ﴿of them﴾ (minhum) ﴿a fear﴾ (khifatan), i.e., fear, because whoever does not eat your food does not keep your covenant of protection (dhimam).

From Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "It occurred to his mind that they were angels sent for punishment."

﴿They said: Do not fear﴾: indeed we are messengers of Allah. It was also said: Jibril wiped the calf, so it stood up and joined its mother.

﴿And they gave him the good news of a learned boy﴾: i.e., one who will reach maturity and will have knowledge. The one given the good news of is Ishaq, according to the majority (al-Jumhur).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 29:

﴿So his wife came forward in a outcry﴾, in a shriek, from "ṣarra al-qalam, wal-bāb" (he made the pen or the door creak). Al-Zajjaj said: "ṣarratin" means intense crying out here, and its position is in the accusative, as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "she came crying out loud." It was also said: she began to shriek, and her "ṣarrah" was her saying: "Woe is me!"

﴿and she struck her face﴾, she slapped with the spread of her hands. It was also said: she struck her forehead with the tips of her fingers, in the manner of one who is astonished.

﴿And she said: "An old woman, barren!"﴾, meaning: I am an old woman, so how could I bear a child?! As He said in another place: ﴿"Shall I bear a child when I am an old woman and this is my husband, an old man?"﴾ [Hud: 72]

Qur'anic quotations: "They said: Thus (it is)." The meaning is: like that which We said, and informed you of.

"Your Lord said." That is: We only inform you about God (Exalted), and God is capable of what you find improbable.

"Indeed He is the All-Wise" in His action, "the All-Knowing," so nothing is hidden from Him.

It is narrated that Gabriel said to her, when she found it improbable: "Look at the roof of your house," so she looked, and behold, its beams were in leaf and bearing fruit.

And when he (Abraham) realized that they were angels, and that they do not descend except by the command of God as messengers for certain matters:

﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ That is: What is your affair? And what is your purpose? And for what were you sent? ﴿O messengers﴾ — were you sent with glad tidings alone, or for another matter, or for both?

Quran verse in ﴿ ﴾ markers:

﴿They said: "Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals."﴾ That is, the people of Lut.

ظ
﴿That We may send down upon them stones of clay﴾. He means sijjil, which is clay that has been baked, as bricks are baked, until it became as hard as stones.

[Musawwamah]: marked, from "al-sawmah," which means a mark or sign; on each stone was the name of the one who would be destroyed by it,

[ʿinda rabbika]: in His dominion and authority,

[lil-musrifin]: He named them "those who exceed the bounds" (musrifun), just as He named them "transgressors" (ʿadun), because of their excess and their aggression in their deeds, since they were not content with what had been permitted to them.

﴿So We brought out those who were in it﴾, in the town, though it has not been mentioned before, because it was well known,

﴿of the believers﴾, meaning Lut (Lot) and those who believed in him.

﴿So We found there not any house of the Muslims other than one house.﴾ That is: other than a household of people. In this is evidence that faith (īmān) and submission (islām) are one and the same, because the angels called them "believers" (mu'minīn) and "Muslims" (muslimīn) here.

"And We left therein" — in their towns —

"a sign for those who fear the painful punishment" — a mark by which those who fear take warning, as opposed to those whose hearts are hardened. It was said: it is black, foul-smelling water.

ï»؟**And in Musa (Moses) [too there is a sign]**, coordinated with "and in the earth are signs," or with His words "and We left therein a sign," in the sense of "and We placed in Musa a sign," like the poet's words:

"I fed her chaff and cold water..."

**﴿When We sent him to Pharaoh with a clear authority﴾**, with a manifest proof, namely the hand and the staff.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 51, verse 39:

(p-٣٧٨)﴿So he turned away﴾, i.e., he turned away from belief,

﴿with his pillar﴾, meaning with what he relied on of his troops and his dominion. And "al-Rukn" (the pillar, support): that on which a person leans, of wealth and troops,

﴿and said, "A sorcerer"﴾, i.e., he is a sorcerer,

﴿or a madman"﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 52]

Verse 40: ﴿So We seized him and his hosts, and cast them into the sea, and he was blameworthy.﴾ (He) came with that for which he was blamed, because of his disbelief and his obstinacy. The description of Yunus (peace be upon him) with this word appears in His saying: ﴿Then the whale swallowed him, and he was blameworthy﴾ [al-Saffat: 142], because the causes of blame differ, and according to their difference the measures of blame differ. The one who commits disbelief is blameworthy in proportion to it, and the one who commits a major sin, a minor sin, or a slip is likewise. The clause introduced by the waw is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "fa-akhadhnahu" (We seized him).

In Ad too (there is a sign), when We sent upon them the barren wind. It is the one in which there is no good, neither bringing rain nor fertilizing trees, and it is the wind of destruction. Its identity has been disputed, and the most apparent view is that it is the dabur (the west wind), because of the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "I was made victorious by the saba (the east wind), and Ad were destroyed by the dabur."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 42:

﴿مَا تَذَرُ مِن شَيْءٍ أَتَتْ عَلَيْهِ إِلَّا جَعَلَتْهُ كَالرَّمِيمِ﴾ ["It leaves nothing it passes over but makes it like rotten dust."] Al-Ramīm (the crumbled, decayed remains) is everything that has become decayed (rumma), i.e., has rotted and crumbled to pieces, whether of bone, plant, or other things. The meaning is: it leaves nothing on which it blows from their souls, their livestock, and their wealth except that it destroys it.
And in Thamud too, there is a sign, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time." Its explanation is His saying: "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days" [Hud: 65].

﴿فَعَتَوْا عَنْ أمْرِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ [They rebelled against the command of their Lord], i.e., they were arrogant about complying with His command.

﴿فَأخَذَتْهُمُ الصاعِقَةُ﴾ [So the thunderbolt seized them]: "al-ṣā'iqa" means the punishment. Every destructive punishment is a ṣā'iqa. "Al-ṣa'qa" [the stroke], "ʿAlī" [a variant reading/example given], and it is the single occurrence of the verbal noun of "ṣa'aqathum al-ṣā'iqa" [the thunderbolt struck them].

﴿وَهم يَنْظُرُونَ﴾ [while they were looking on]: because it happened in daytime, and they were witnessing it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 45:

﴿So they were not able to stand up [against it]﴾. That is: to flee; or it is from their saying, "so-and-so cannot stand up to it" (ma yaqumu bihi), when he is unable to repel it.

﴿And they were not ones who could defend themselves﴾, that is, unable to protect themselves from the punishment; or it was not possible for them to counter Us with the punishment, because the meaning of intisar (defending oneself, retaliating) is confrontation.

﴿And the people of Nuh﴾: meaning, And We destroyed the people of Nuh, because what precedes it indicates it; or "Remember the people of Nuh." And with the genitive (jarr), Abu 'Amr, 'Ali and Hamzah (read it as وَقَوْمِ, "and [in] the people of Nuh"), meaning: and in the people of Nuh there is a sign. Supporting this is the recitation of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud): "and in the people of Nuh."

﴿from before﴾: from before these mentioned ones.

﴿Indeed they were a people who were defiantly disobedient﴾: disbelievers.

**Al-Nasafi's commentary (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 51, verse 47:**

﴿And the heaven﴾: it is in the accusative case, governed by a verb implied by the verb that explains it, ﴿We built it with might﴾, that is, with strength. And "al-aydu" (al-ayd) means strength.

﴿And indeed We are expanding it﴾: that is, We are capable. It is derived from "al-wus'" (al-wus'), which is capacity and ability. And "al-muwsi'" (al-muwsi') means one who is strong in spending. Or it means: "We are expanding [the space] between the heaven and the earth."

"And the earth — We spread it out (farashnaha), We extended it and made it a cradle (mahhadnaha), and it is in the accusative by a suppressed verb, meaning: We spread out the earth, We spread it out,

﴿So how excellent are the Spreaders⁠﴾, We."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 49:

"And of everything We have created pairs, that you may remember."

"And of every thing" — that is, from among the animals.

"We created pairs" — male and female. It is also related from al-Hasan (al-Basri) that he said: "The heaven and the earth, the night and the day, the sun and the moon, the land and the sea, death and life." He enumerated things and said: "Every two of them are a pair." And Allah (Exalted is He) is One (fard), having no like.

"That you may remember" — meaning: We did all of that, the construction of the heaven, the spreading of the earth, and the creation of pairs, so that you may remember, and thus know the Creator and worship Him.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 50:**

﴿So flee to Allah⟩ i.e., from polytheism to belief in Allah, or from obedience to Satan to obedience to the Most Merciful, or from everything other than Him to Him,

﴿Indeed, I am a clear warner to you from Him.﴾

Translation:

"And do not set up another god alongside Allah. Indeed, I am a clear warner to you from Him." The repetition serves emphasis, and prolonging the warning is more forceful.

Qur'anic quotations go in ﴿ ﴾ with plain meaning. Translating.

﴿Thus⦆ — "The matter is like that," and "that" refers to their denying the Messenger and calling him "a sorcerer" or "a madman." Then he (al-Nasafi) explained what was stated in summary by his saying: ﴿Never came to those before them⦆ — from before your people — (p-380) ﴿any messenger but they said⦆ — he is ﴿a sorcerer or a madman⦆. They accused them of sorcery or madness, out of their ignorance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 53:

﴿Have they enjoined this upon one another?﴾ The pronoun in "bihi" (this) refers to the saying. That is: Have the earlier and the later generations enjoined one another upon this saying, until they all said it together, agreeing upon it?! ﴿Nay, they are a people who transgress all bounds.﴾ That is: they did not enjoin it upon one another, because they did not meet in one time; rather, a single cause brought them together, namely tughyan (transgression, overweening rebellion), and tughyan is what impelled them to it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 54:

﴿So turn away from them﴾: that is, turn away from those to whom you have repeatedly conveyed the call, and who did not respond out of obstinacy.

﴿And you are not to be blamed﴾: that is, there is no blame upon you for turning away after you have conveyed the message and exerted your utmost effort in delivering and calling (to the truth).

﴿And remind⁠﴾, that is, admonish with the Qur'an,

﴿for indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾, by increasing them in their knowledge.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 56:

﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me.﴾ As for worship (ʿibadah), if it is taken in its literal sense, then the verse is not general; rather, what is meant by it is the believers from both groups. The evidence for this is the context, namely: ﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:55]; and the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except those among the believers﴾. This is because it is not permissible that He create for worship those of whom He knows that they will not believe, for if He created them for worship and willed worship from them, it must come to pass from them; and when they do not believe, it is known that He created them for Hell, as He said: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind﴾ [al-Aʿraf 7:179]. It has been said: "except that I might command them to worship," and this is reported from ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him). It has also been said: "except that they might be servants to Me." The preferable view is that worship be understood as tawhid (monotheism), for Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Every instance of worship in the Qur'an is tawhid." All of them will affirm His oneness in the Hereafter, since it is known that all the disbelievers will be believers who affirm His oneness in the Hereafter. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Then their trial will be only that they say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:23]. Yes, some did associate partners in this world, but the duration of this world, in comparison with eternity, is less than a day. If someone buys a slave and says, "I bought him only for writing," he is truthful in his saying, "I bought him only for writing," even if he uses him for another task on some day of his life.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 57:

﴿I do not desire any provision from them﴾: I did not create them so that they would provide for themselves, or for any one of My servants.

﴿Nor do I desire that they should feed Me﴾. Tha'lab said: "That they should feed My servants." This is an idafa of specification (idafat takhsis, a construction that singles out a particular referent), like the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) relating from Allah (Exalted is He): "Whoever honours a believer has honoured Me, and whoever harms a believer has harmed Me."

Indeed, Allah is the Provider (al-Razzaq), the Possessor of Power (dhu al-quwwah), the Firm (al-Matin) (Q. 51:58).

Al-Nasafi says: "the Firm" (al-shadid al-quwwah, i.e., of intense strength). "Al-Matin," with a raised vowel (bi-l-raf'), is an attribute (sifah) of "dhu" (the one possessing). Al-A'mash read it with a lowered vowel (bi-l-jarr), as an attribute of "al-quwwah" (strength), according to the interpretation of "al-iqtidar" (capability, power).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 51, verse 59:

﴿Indeed, for those who wronged﴾: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), by denying him, from among the people of Makkah,

﴿a portion like the portion of their companions﴾: a share of the punishment of Allah, like the share of their companions and their counterparts from the destroyed generations. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) said: "al-dhanub" (dhanūb, portion), in the language, means the share.

﴿So let them not ask Me to hasten﴾: the descent of the punishment. This is a response to al-Nadr (al-Nadr ibn al-Harith) and his companions, when they asked for the punishment to be hastened.

﴿So woe to those who disbelieve, from their Day which they are promised.﴾ That is, from the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: from the Day of Badr.

The words "liya'buduni" (﴿that they may worship Me﴾), "an yut'imuni" (﴿that they feed Me﴾), and "fala yasta'jiluni" (﴿so let them not seek to hasten Me﴾) are read with a final ya' (ي) in both pausal and continuous recitation, according to Ya'qub. Sahl agreed with him in continuous recitation. The rest of the readers read them without the ya'.
